title: Level 4: External Interrupts (INT0 / INT1)
aim: To configure the ATmega328P's hardware External Interrupt pins (INT0 on PD2 and INT1 on PD3) to trigger an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) on a button press, without polling the pin in the main loop.
objective: Understand the interrupt subsystem of AVR — EICRA (trigger sense), EIMSK (enable mask), the global interrupt enable bit (sei), and writing ISRs. Compare interrupt-driven input handling versus polling.
theory:
What Is an Interrupt?

An interrupt is a hardware signal that instantly suspends the CPU's current execution, saves its state (all registers and the Program Counter onto the stack), and jumps to a special function called an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR). When the ISR returns (via the RETI instruction), the CPU restores its saved state and resumes exactly where it left off. This mechanism allows the processor to respond to real-world events (button presses, timer overflows, serial data) in microseconds, without wasting cycles polling in a loop.

External Interrupt Pins: INT0 and INT1

The ATmega328P has two dedicated external interrupt pins: INT0 (PD2 = Arduino Pin 2) and INT1 (PD3 = Arduino Pin 3). Unlike pin-change interrupts, INT0 and INT1 have selectable trigger sense — you configure whether the interrupt fires on a LOW level, a logic change, a falling edge, or a rising edge.

EICRA — External Interrupt Control Register A

The trigger sense for INT0 and INT1 is set via EICRA:

  • ISC01:ISC00 (bits 1:0) — control INT0 sense: 00=LOW level, 01=any change, 10=falling edge, 11=rising edge
  • ISC11:ISC10 (bits 3:2) — same options for INT1

To detect a falling edge on INT0: EICRA |= (1 << ISC01); (ISC01=1, ISC00=0 → 10 = falling edge).

EIMSK — External Interrupt Mask Register

Setting a bit in EIMSK enables that interrupt line: EIMSK |= (1 << INT0);. If the corresponding bit is clear, the interrupt is masked (ignored) even if the pin triggers.

Global Interrupt Enable — sei()

Even after configuring EICRA and EIMSK, no interrupt fires until the I-bit (Global Interrupt Enable) in SREG is set. The intrinsic function sei() sets this bit. Its counterpart cli() clears it, temporarily disabling all interrupts (useful for atomic register accesses).

Writing the ISR

ISRs for external interrupts are written using the ISR()<avr/interrupt.h>:

ISR(INT0_vect) {
  // code runs on INT0 trigger
}

Key ISR rules: keep them short and fast — no delays, no blocking calls. Use volatile global flags to communicate results back to the main loop.

Polling vs Interrupts

PollingInterrupts
CPU constantly checks pin state in a loopCPU is notified automatically by hardware
Wastes CPU cycles when nothing happensCPU free to do other work or sleep
Simple to codeSlightly more complex setup
Response latency = polling periodResponse latency = 4–7 clock cycles

pretest.question: Which register controls the trigger sense (edge/level) for INT0 and INT1?
pretest.explanation: EICRA (External Interrupt Control Register A) holds ISC0x bits for INT0 and ISC1x bits for INT1, selecting the trigger condition.

pretest.question: Which register enables or disables INT0 and INT1 interrupts?
pretest.explanation: EIMSK (External Interrupt Mask Register) has INT0 bit (bit 0) and INT1 bit (bit 1). Setting them enables the respective interrupt lines.

pretest.question: What bit combination in EICRA sets INT0 to trigger on a FALLING EDGE?
pretest.explanation: The AVR datasheet defines: ISC01=1, ISC00=0 → falling edge. ISC01=1, ISC00=1 → rising edge.

pretest.question: What is the function of sei() in AVR firmware?
options: Set the global interrupt enable I-bit in SREG
pretest.explanation: sei() (Set Enable Interrupts) sets the I (Global Interrupt Enable) bit in the Status Register (SREG), allowing all enabled interrupts to fire.

pretest.question: Where must the INT0 ISR function be declared?
options: As an ordinary C function called int0_handler
pretest.explanation: The ISR macro from <avr/interrupt.h> creates the correctly named interrupt vector function that the hardware jumps to when INT0 fires.

pretest.question: Why should ISRs be kept short and free of delay functions?
options: Blocking inside an ISR prevents other interrupts and main loop from running
pretest.explanation: While inside an ISR, global interrupts are disabled. Blocking with delays prevents the system from responding to anything else during that time.

pretest.question: What is the typical ISR response latency on AVR (from event to first ISR instruction)?
pretest.explanation: AVR interrupts have a fixed latency of 4 cycles to complete the current instruction + push state + jump to the ISR vector.

pretest.question: Why must variables shared between ISRs and the main loop be declared 'volatile'?
options: To prevent the compiler from caching the value in a register across ISR calls
pretest.explanation: Without volatile, the compiler may cache the variable in a CPU register and never re-read it from SRAM, missing updates made by the ISR.

pretest.question: Which Arduino Uno pin corresponds to INT0?
pretest.explanation: INT0 is mapped to Port D pin 2 (PD2), which is Arduino Uno Digital Pin 2.

pretest.question: What happens when an ISR returns?
options: CPU resumes execution at the exact point where it was interrupted
pretest.explanation: The RETI instruction (Return from Interrupt) restores the saved PC and all CPU registers from the stack, resuming execution seamlessly.

procedure: Include headers: #include <avr/io.h> and #include <avr/interrupt.h>. Define a volatile flag variable: volatile uint8_t buttonPressed = 0;. This will be set by the ISR and read by main.
Configure the LED pin as output: DDRB |= (1 << PB5);. Configure INT0 pin (PD2) as input: DDRD &= ~(1 << PD2);. Enable its pull-up resistor: PORTD |= (1 << PD2);.
Configure INT0 to trigger on a falling edge (button press creates HIGH→LOW transition). Set ISC01=1, ISC00=0 in EICRA: EICRA |= (1 << ISC01); — leave ISC00 as 0 (default).
Enable the INT0 interrupt line by setting bit INT0 in EIMSK: EIMSK |= (1 << INT0);. The interrupt is now armed but will not fire until global interrupts are enabled.
Enable global interrupts: sei();. From this point, any falling edge on PD2 will immediately invoke the INT0 ISR, even from inside the main loop.

In the main loop while(1), check the volatile flag: if (buttonPressed) { PORTB ^= (1 << PB5); buttonPressed = 0; }. This pattern — set flag in ISR, act in main — is the standard interrupt-safe design.

Write the ISR outside of any function: ISR(INT0_vect) { buttonPressed = 1; }. The ISR simply sets the flag. Hardware debounce is not included here — if needed, disable INT0 in the ISR and re-enable it after a timer delay.

Wire the circuit: push button between Pin 2 (PD2) and GND. LED with 330 Ω resistor on Pin 13 (PB5). Compile and flash. Each button press should toggle the LED visually, with the main loop free to run other tasks between presses.

posttest.question: What is the key difference between INT0/INT1 and Pin Change Interrupts (PCINT)?
options: INT0/INT1 support configurable edge/level sensing; PCINTs only detect any change
posttest.explanation: INT0 and INT1 allow choosing falling, rising, any-change, or LOW-level triggers. Pin Change Interrupts (PCINT) only fire on any logic change and share one ISR per port group.

posttest.question: If you set ISC01=1 and ISC00=1 in EICRA for INT0, what is the trigger condition?
posttest.explanation: ISC01=1, ISC00=1 configures INT0 for rising edge (LOW→HIGH transition), per the AVR datasheet Table 12-1.

posttest.question: What does cli() do, and when would you use it?
options: Disables global interrupts — used to protect atomic multi-register operations
posttest.explanation: cli() clears the I-bit in SREG, disabling all interrupts. Used to protect critical sections where a partial register update mid-ISR would cause data corruption.

posttest.question: What happens if INT0 fires while already inside the INT0 ISR (without sei() inside the ISR)?
options: The trigger is latched and executes after ISR returns
posttest.explanation: The interrupt flag is set in hardware even while interrupts are disabled. After RETI restores the I-bit, the pending interrupt fires immediately.

posttest.question: Which SREG bit must be 1 for ANY interrupt to fire?
posttest.explanation: The I-bit (bit 7) of SREG is the global interrupt gate. All configured interrupts require this bit to be set (done via sei()).

posttest.question: What is the stack used for during an interrupt?
options: Saving the Program Counter and CPU registers before jumping to ISR
posttest.explanation: On interrupt, the AVR pushes the current PC and all 32 general-purpose registers onto the SRAM stack before jumping to the ISR vector.

posttest.question: What is a watchdog timer used for?
options: Resetting the MCU if software hangs and fails to clear the WDT
posttest.explanation: The Watchdog Timer auto-resets the MCU if the software fails to periodically 'pet' it (clear it), recovering from infinite loops or crashes.

posttest.question: Why is 'volatile' required for a flag variable shared between ISR and main loop?
options: To prevent compiler from optimizing away reads from SRAM
posttest.explanation: The compiler may optimize a non-volatile shared variable by keeping it in a register and never re-reading SRAM. The ISR modifies SRAM, but main never sees the update.

posttest.question: What is the difference between PORTB and PINB?
options: PORTB drives outputs / enables pull-ups; PINB reads real-time pin voltages
posttest.explanation: PORTB is the output data register (also controls pull-ups on inputs). PINB is the pin input register — it reads the actual current voltage on each Port B pin.

posttest.question: In an ISR, interrupts are automatically:
options: Disabled until ISR returns (RETI restores I-bit)
posttest.explanation: The AVR hardware clears the I-bit in SREG upon entering any ISR, preventing nested interrupts. RETI instruction re-enables them on return.

feedback: Superb! You've harnessed the interrupt subsystem — one of the most powerful tools in embedded systems. Interrupt-driven design is the foundation of all responsive firmware, from keyboards to motor controllers to communication stacks.
